by Max Dubler
Introduction
It should not take a supermajority of voters to raise revenues for local schools, infrastructure, and public safety.
Analysis
Background
Proposition 13, passed by voters in 1978, amended the state constitution to cap property tax rates at 1% of a property’s assessed value; limit annual increases in assessed value; require a ⅔ supermajority vote in the legislature to raise state taxes; and require a ⅔ voter approval for local “special taxes” earmarked for a specific purpose.
In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional supermajority requirements were written to constrain governments , not the people’s initiative power, and that “special” taxes that have been proposed via citizen initiatives can pass with a standard 50%+1 majority.
In 2022, Los Angeles voters passed Measure ULA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_ULA), which dramatically raised the transfer tax (https://finance.lacity.gov/faq/measure-ula) on real estate transactions over $5 million to up to 5.5%. Advertised to voters as a “mansion tax,” it has mostly affected the sales of apartment buildings and other commercial properties, leading to a very significant slowdown (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/the-unintended-consequences-of-measure-ula/) in large commercial property transactions and new housing construction (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/taxing-tomorrow-measure-ulas-impact-on-multifamily-housing-production-and-potential-reforms/). San Francisco (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2020-11/sf-prop-i-transfer-tax-increase) and Santa Monica (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publication/230301-7087-santa-monica-measure-gs) have also passed significant transfer tax increases, with similar negative effects for housing.
Earlier this year, The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers’ Association (HJTA), which sponsored Prop 13 back in 1978, collected signatures for a ballot measure (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) that would do two things: restore the 66% supermajority requirement for special taxes and limit local transfer taxes to 0.055%. In June, the state legislature attempted to make a deal with the HJTA to keep this measure off the ballot by reforming transfer taxes, a laudable goal that we supported (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/06/mansion-tax-ballot-measure-deal/). That effort was not successful: negotiations broke down at the 11th hour (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/). When the dust settled, a deal was struck to have the legislature put the voter threshold piece on the ballot by itself without the transfer tax reforms. That is Prop 43.
What does this do?
Raises the threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing voter-approved special taxes from 50%+1 to 66% and prohibits local governments from taxing real estate according to its value, except under narrow circumstances.
How will this affect housing?
Prop 43 will impact housing production by making it harder for local governments to raise revenue for housing-related purposes like infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation.
Passing Prop 43 would also give local governments an even stronger incentive to charge very high impact fees for new housing (https://cayimby.org/reports/the-impact-of-fees/), which will increase the price of new homes and exacerbate the housing shortage.
Recommendation: No.
Kneecapping local governments’ ability to raise revenue is bad news for housing and infrastructure. Further, the HJTA should not be rewarded for using housing affordability as a Trojan horse to put unrelated tax cuts on the ballot.
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), initiative text (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22), “no” endorsement from transit advocacy group Seamless Bay Area (https://www.seamlessbayarea.org/blog/2026/7/10/prop-43-the-anti-tax-ballot-measure-and-transit-funding).

Prop
43
CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

Proposition 43: No
September 23, 2026
Max Dubler
Share
Share this page on Twitter (https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-43-2026%2F&text=Proposition+43%3A+No)
Share this page on Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-43-2026%2F&t=Proposition%2043:%20No)
Share this page via Email (mailto:?subject=Proposition+43%3A+No+-+California+YIMBY&body=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-43-2026%2F)
by Max Dubler
Introduction
It should not take a supermajority of voters to raise revenues for local schools, infrastructure, and public safety.
Analysis
Background
Proposition 13, passed by voters in 1978, amended the state constitution to cap property tax rates at 1% of a property’s assessed value; limit annual increases in assessed value; require a ⅔ supermajority vote in the legislature to raise state taxes; and require a ⅔ voter approval for local “special taxes” earmarked for a specific purpose.
In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional supermajority requirements were written to constrain governments , not the people’s initiative power, and that “special” taxes that have been proposed via citizen initiatives can pass with a standard 50%+1 majority.
In 2022, Los Angeles voters passed Measure ULA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_ULA), which dramatically raised the transfer tax (https://finance.lacity.gov/faq/measure-ula) on real estate transactions over $5 million to up to 5.5%. Advertised to voters as a “mansion tax,” it has mostly affected the sales of apartment buildings and other commercial properties, leading to a very significant slowdown (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/the-unintended-consequences-of-measure-ula/) in large commercial property transactions and new housing construction (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/taxing-tomorrow-measure-ulas-impact-on-multifamily-housing-production-and-potential-reforms/). San Francisco (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2020-11/sf-prop-i-transfer-tax-increase) and Santa Monica (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publication/230301-7087-santa-monica-measure-gs) have also passed significant transfer tax increases, with similar negative effects for housing.
Earlier this year, The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers’ Association (HJTA), which sponsored Prop 13 back in 1978, collected signatures for a ballot measure (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) that would do two things: restore the 66% supermajority requirement for special taxes and limit local transfer taxes to 0.055%. In June, the state legislature attempted to make a deal with the HJTA to keep this measure off the ballot by reforming transfer taxes, a laudable goal that we supported (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/06/mansion-tax-ballot-measure-deal/). That effort was not successful: negotiations broke down at the 11th hour (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/). When the dust settled, a deal was struck to have the legislature put the voter threshold piece on the ballot by itself without the transfer tax reforms. That is Prop 43.
What does this do?
Raises the threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing voter-approved special taxes from 50%+1 to 66% and prohibits local governments from taxing real estate according to its value, except under narrow circumstances.
How will this affect housing?
Prop 43 will impact housing production by making it harder for local governments to raise revenue for housing-related purposes like infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation.
Passing Prop 43 would also give local governments an even stronger incentive to charge very high impact fees for new housing (https://cayimby.org/reports/the-impact-of-fees/), which will increase the price of new homes and exacerbate the housing shortage.
Recommendation: No.
Kneecapping local governments’ ability to raise revenue is bad news for housing and infrastructure. Further, the HJTA should not be rewarded for using housing affordability as a Trojan horse to put unrelated tax cuts on the ballot.
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), initiative text (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22), “no” endorsement from transit advocacy group Seamless Bay Area (https://www.seamlessbayarea.org/blog/2026/7/10/prop-43-the-anti-tax-ballot-measure-and-transit-funding).

by Max Dubler
Introduction
It should not take a supermajority of voters to raise revenues for local schools, infrastructure, and public safety.
Analysis
Background
Proposition 13, passed by voters in 1978, amended the state constitution to cap property tax rates at 1% of a property’s assessed value; limit annual increases in assessed value; require a ⅔ supermajority vote in the legislature to raise state taxes; and require a ⅔ voter approval for local “special taxes” earmarked for a specific purpose.
In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional supermajority requirements were written to constrain governments , not the people’s initiative power, and that “special” taxes that have been proposed via citizen initiatives can pass with a standard 50%+1 majority.
In 2022, Los Angeles voters passed Measure ULA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_ULA), which dramatically raised the transfer tax (https://finance.lacity.gov/faq/measure-ula) on real estate transactions over $5 million to up to 5.5%. Advertised to voters as a “mansion tax,” it has mostly affected the sales of apartment buildings and other commercial properties, leading to a very significant slowdown (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/the-unintended-consequences-of-measure-ula/) in large commercial property transactions and new housing construction (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/taxing-tomorrow-measure-ulas-impact-on-multifamily-housing-production-and-potential-reforms/). San Francisco (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2020-11/sf-prop-i-transfer-tax-increase) and Santa Monica (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publication/230301-7087-santa-monica-measure-gs) have also passed significant transfer tax increases, with similar negative effects for housing.
Earlier this year, The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers’ Association (HJTA), which sponsored Prop 13 back in 1978, collected signatures for a ballot measure (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) that would do two things: restore the 66% supermajority requirement for special taxes and limit local transfer taxes to 0.055%. In June, the state legislature attempted to make a deal with the HJTA to keep this measure off the ballot by reforming transfer taxes, a laudable goal that we supported (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/06/mansion-tax-ballot-measure-deal/). That effort was not successful: negotiations broke down at the 11th hour (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/). When the dust settled, a deal was struck to have the legislature put the voter threshold piece on the ballot by itself without the transfer tax reforms. That is Prop 43.
What does this do?
Raises the threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing voter-approved special taxes from 50%+1 to 66% and prohibits local governments from taxing real estate according to its value, except under narrow circumstances.
How will this affect housing?
Prop 43 will impact housing production by making it harder for local governments to raise revenue for housing-related purposes like infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation.
Passing Prop 43 would also give local governments an even stronger incentive to charge very high impact fees for new housing (https://cayimby.org/reports/the-impact-of-fees/), which will increase the price of new homes and exacerbate the housing shortage.
Recommendation: No.
Kneecapping local governments’ ability to raise revenue is bad news for housing and infrastructure. Further, the HJTA should not be rewarded for using housing affordability as a Trojan horse to put unrelated tax cuts on the ballot.
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), initiative text (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22), “no” endorsement from transit advocacy group Seamless Bay Area (https://www.seamlessbayarea.org/blog/2026/7/10/prop-43-the-anti-tax-ballot-measure-and-transit-funding).

Prop
43
CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.
Vote NO

Proposition 43: No

by Max Dubler
Introduction
It should not take a supermajority of voters to raise revenues for local schools, infrastructure, and public safety.
Analysis
Background
Proposition 13, passed by voters in 1978, amended the state constitution to cap property tax rates at 1% of a property’s assessed value; limit annual increases in assessed value; require a ⅔ supermajority vote in the legislature to raise state taxes; and require a ⅔ voter approval for local “special taxes” earmarked for a specific purpose.
In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional supermajority requirements were written to constrain governments , not the people’s initiative power, and that “special” taxes that have been proposed via citizen initiatives can pass with a standard 50%+1 majority.
In 2022, Los Angeles voters passed Measure ULA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_ULA), which dramatically raised the transfer tax (https://finance.lacity.gov/faq/measure-ula) on real estate transactions over $5 million to up to 5.5%. Advertised to voters as a “mansion tax,” it has mostly affected the sales of apartment buildings and other commercial properties, leading to a very significant slowdown (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/the-unintended-consequences-of-measure-ula/) in large commercial property transactions and new housing construction (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/taxing-tomorrow-measure-ulas-impact-on-multifamily-housing-production-and-potential-reforms/). San Francisco (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2020-11/sf-prop-i-transfer-tax-increase) and Santa Monica (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publication/230301-7087-santa-monica-measure-gs) have also passed significant transfer tax increases, with similar negative effects for housing.
Earlier this year, The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers’ Association (HJTA), which sponsored Prop 13 back in 1978, collected signatures for a ballot measure (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) that would do two things: restore the 66% supermajority requirement for special taxes and limit local transfer taxes to 0.055%. In June, the state legislature attempted to make a deal with the HJTA to keep this measure off the ballot by reforming transfer taxes, a laudable goal that we supported (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/06/mansion-tax-ballot-measure-deal/). That effort was not successful: negotiations broke down at the 11th hour (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/). When the dust settled, a deal was struck to have the legislature put the voter threshold piece on the ballot by itself without the transfer tax reforms. That is Prop 43.
What does this do?
Raises the threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing voter-approved special taxes from 50%+1 to 66% and prohibits local governments from taxing real estate according to its value, except under narrow circumstances.
How will this affect housing?
Prop 43 will impact housing production by making it harder for local governments to raise revenue for housing-related purposes like infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation.
Passing Prop 43 would also give local governments an even stronger incentive to charge very high impact fees for new housing (https://cayimby.org/reports/the-impact-of-fees/), which will increase the price of new homes and exacerbate the housing shortage.
Recommendation: No.
Kneecapping local governments’ ability to raise revenue is bad news for housing and infrastructure. Further, the HJTA should not be rewarded for using housing affordability as a Trojan horse to put unrelated tax cuts on the ballot.
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), initiative text (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22), “no” endorsement from transit advocacy group Seamless Bay Area (https://www.seamlessbayarea.org/blog/2026/7/10/prop-43-the-anti-tax-ballot-measure-and-transit-funding).

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Local Taxes: Limitation (Proposition 43)
August 2026
TAXPAYERS ASSOCIATION POSITION SUPPORT
Rationale for Position:
Proposition 43 would extend to citizen-initiated local special taxes the same two-thirds vote
requirement that already applies to special taxes referred by local governments, closing the
disparity the Upland decision opened, and the record since 2017 shows the gap it closes is not
hypothetical: roughly two dozen local special taxes have been enacted statewide by simple
majority under the current rule. Of note, the empirical research on supermajority tax rules
generally is mixed as to whether such thresholds meaningfully change tax levels, so the
recommendation rests on the principle that citizen-initiated special taxes should receive the same
treatment as agency-initiated ones — and not serve as a route to bypass the two-thirds threshold
— rather than on a confident revenue prediction.
Title: Local taxes: limitation. Ballot designation: Proposition 43. Staff to confirm the certified
ballot title, label, and summary against the Secretary of State’s Voter Information Guide once
published.
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment
22, authored by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks; approved by a two-thirds vote of the
Legislature on June 25, 2026, and enacted as Resolution Chapter 132, Statutes of 2026); adds
Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution.
Vote: November 2026 Statewide General Election
Status: Placed on the November 2026 ballot directly by the Legislature; no citizen signature-
gathering was required or occurred.
Description: Beginning January 1, 2027, requires approval by two-thirds of the electorate
before any local government — including the electorate acting through the citizen-initiative
power — may impose, extend, or increase a special tax, closing what is commonly called the
“Upland loophole.” Separately reinforces the existing constitutional prohibition on local ad
valorem property taxes outside the framework the Constitution already permits.
Fiscal Impact: Staff has not identified an official Legislative Analyst’s Office or Department
of Finance fiscal estimate for this measure as of this draft; Staff to obtain the estimate prepared
for the Voter Information Guide once published. Because the measure applies only
prospectively to future local special taxes, any fiscal effect would take the form of foregone
local revenue relative to current law, not a change to any tax now in effect.
SDtaxpayers.org • 2
Background
Proposition 13 (1978) capped the property tax rate at one percent of assessed value, limited
annual increases in assessed value to two percent until a change of ownership, and required a
two-thirds vote of local electorates for local special taxes — those whose revenue is legally
dedicated to a specific purpose, as distinct from general taxes that flow to a jurisdiction’s general
fund. That requirement was refined by Proposition 218 (1996). In 2017, the California Supreme
Court’s decision in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland created uncertainty about
whether the two-thirds requirement applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by citizen
initiative rather than by a local government; several lower courts subsequently upheld citizen-
initiated special taxes adopted by simple majority, opening what is commonly called the “Upland
loophole.”
The record since 2017 gives voters a concrete basis for weighing this measure rather than a
purely hypothetical one. By one count, cities and counties have enacted roughly two dozen
special-tax measures statewide by margins of less than two-thirds since Upland, including parcel,
sales, and gross-receipts taxes dedicated to schools, parks, street repairs, transit, and housing,
placed on the ballot by proponents ranging from homeless-services advocates and environmental
groups to organized labor. Los Angeles’s 2022 Measure ULA, a tax on high-value real estate
transfers, is the best-known example. Opponents of this measure have pointed to more recent
examples they say illustrate what a two-thirds requirement would foreclose going forward:
Alameda County’s November 2025 Measure B, a parcel tax supporting Washington Hospital,
passed with 64.7 percent of the vote, and Sonoma County’s March 2024 Measure H, a sales tax
funding fire and disaster response, passed with 61 percent — both comfortably above a simple
majority but short of two-thirds.
Broader research on supermajority requirements for taxation is relevant but not squarely on
point. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, reviewing states that require a legislative
supermajority to raise state taxes, has found that those states have historically levied taxes at
levels nearly identical, on average, to states without such a requirement, suggesting such rules do
not reliably reduce the level of taxation over the long run; other research reaches more favorable
conclusions for supermajority rules, and the evidence is genuinely mixed. That research,
however, examines a two-thirds vote of a legislature to raise state taxes, a different mechanism
than this measure, which asks whether voters themselves must clear a two-thirds threshold to
approve a local special tax. Direct empirical evidence on this specific mechanism is limited, in
part because the simple-majority pathway it would close has existed only since 2017.
The Proposal
Proposition 43 reached the ballot through an unusual path. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers
Association had qualified a broader citizen initiative for the November 2026 ballot that
combined a two-thirds fix for the Upland loophole with a cap on local real estate transfer taxes
SDtaxpayers.org • 3
and the retroactive voiding of existing transfer taxes above that cap, including Measure ULA. In
the closing days before the ballot was finalized, the Legislature passed this measure and
rescinded a prior “poison pill” provision in exchange for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers
Association withdrawing its broader initiative; the transfer-tax provisions were dropped in that
exchange and do not appear here.
The measure adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution. It raises no
revenue and imposes no new tax. Its principal provisions are:
● Two-thirds vote for all local special taxes: beginning January 1, 2027, no local government
— including the electorate of a local government acting through the initiative power — may
impose, extend, or increase a special tax without approval by two-thirds of those voting,
eliminating the distinction the Upland decision had opened between government-proposed
and citizen-initiated special taxes.
● Ad valorem property tax prohibition: bars any local government — and, again, the
electorate acting by initiative — from imposing a new ad valorem tax (a tax based on a
property’s value) on real property beyond what the Constitution already permits under
Article XIII A and Article XIII D. In practical terms, this forecloses using the citizen-
initiative route the Upland decision opened to enact a property tax that would sidestep
Proposition 13’s one-percent rate cap — a more direct protection of Proposition 13’s central
limit than the special-tax threshold itself.
● Prospective application only: the measure applies to special taxes imposed, extended, or
increased on or after January 1, 2027 and does not affect any existing voter-approved special
tax. Because the measure reaches the extension of a special tax, however, an existing
temporary special tax that was adopted by simple majority would face the two-thirds
threshold when it later comes up for renewal, so the measure’s practical reach extends over
time to the many local special taxes now on a fixed sunset.
The measure does not cap or otherwise affect local real estate transfer taxes, and does not
retroactively affect any existing tax. It also does not change Proposition 13's one-percent
property tax rate cap, its two-percent annual assessment-growth limit, or the property tax base
that funds schools and local services.
Taxpayers Association Findings
Fiscal Impact on Taxpayers
No official fiscal estimate specific to this measure was available to staff as of this draft.
Qualitatively, the roughly two dozen special-tax measures enacted statewide since 2017 by less
than two-thirds — including the two specific examples described above under Background,
which passed with 64.7 percent and 61 percent — give a rough sense of what is at stake: a
meaningful share of future local special taxes that would pass by simple majority would fail to
reach a two-thirds threshold, translating into foregone local revenue for the agencies that would
SDtaxpayers.org • 4
have sponsored them, relative to continuing under current law. Staff has not located an aggregate
estimate of how much revenue such measures have generated statewide to date, information the
Board may wish to request before finalizing a position.
Governance Impact
This measure presents a single central governance tradeoff. The Association’s preference is that
citizen-initiated special taxes receive the same treatment as those referred by a local government
— namely the two-thirds threshold that has applied to agency-proposed special taxes since
Proposition 13 — rather than allowing the citizen-initiative power to become a route for
approving dedicated taxes by simple majority, including taxes that fund services traditionally
supported by the general fund. Closing the Upland loophole restores that parity and advances the
principle that a dedicated tax increase should command broad consensus regardless of who
places it on the ballot. Set against that is the principle of local control and local fiscal self-
determination: the measure constrains the ability of a simple majority of local voters to tax
themselves for services they choose, whether that tax is proposed by a local government or by
citizen initiative. The record of roughly two dozen measures passed by less than two-thirds since
2017 shows this is a live, regularly exercised form of local decision-making, not a rare or
theoretical one.
Areas of Concern
The principal concern is the local-control tension described above: opponents may frame a two-
thirds requirement for citizen-initiated special taxes as a restriction on local majorities’ ability to
fund community priorities they have chosen for themselves, particularly for services such as
transit, fire protection, and homelessness response that have relied on the simple-majority
pathway in recent years.
Second, voters should understand what this measure does not reach. In its recent review of local
general-purpose sales tax measures, the Taxpayers Association has flagged a standing concern
distinct from anything at issue here: a city council places a general tax on the ballot, which
requires only a simple majority and legally dedicates the revenue to nothing, while the
accompanying campaign describes a specific list of infrastructure or service priorities the money
is said to fund. None of that is legally binding, and a future council remains free to redirect the
revenue to any lawful purpose without further voter approval. This measure does not close that
gap. It raises the vote threshold only for special taxes — those that legally dedicate revenue to a
stated purpose — and only to equalize the citizen-initiative and government-referred paths within
that category; it leaves the general-tax path, and a council’s choice to use general-tax financing
while marketing it as if it were dedicated, entirely untouched. A city that wants the simple-
majority threshold need only continue structuring its measure as a general tax.
Third, the empirical case for taxpayer savings is less certain than the policy argument for broad
consensus. Research on supermajority requirements to raise taxes is mixed, and the closest
SDtaxpayers.org • 5
available evidence concerns a different mechanism (legislative supermajorities for state tax
increases) than the one this measure proposes (voter supermajorities for local special taxes).
Voters should support or oppose this measure on the strength of the consensus-threshold
principle itself, not on an assured expectation that it will meaningfully lower local tax burdens.
Proponents
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, through proponent Jon Coupal, supports the measure
as achieving the two-thirds-threshold protection it has long sought for local special taxes.
General taxpayer and business organizations that favor a two-thirds threshold for local special
taxes, such as the California Taxpayers Association and the California Business Roundtable,
would be expected to support the measure on the same grounds, though Staff has not confirmed
formal positions. Commercial real estate and development interests that have separately
advocated for capping or eliminating local real estate transfer taxes are not understood to be
significant funders of this measure, since it does not address transfer taxes.
Opponents
Local government officials and associations and public-sector unions can be expected to oppose
raising the vote threshold for citizen-initiated special taxes, on the ground that it restricts local
voters' ability to fund local priorities by simple majority. Transit advocates, including the
organization Seamless Bay Area, have opposed the measure specifically on the ground that it
would make future transit funding measures harder to pass, citing Alameda County's Measure B
and Sonoma County's Measure H, described above, as examples of recent measures that would
not have cleared a two-thirds threshold.

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Local Taxes: Limitation (Proposition 43)
August 2026
TAXPAYERS ASSOCIATION POSITION SUPPORT
Rationale for Position:
Proposition 43 would extend to citizen-initiated local special taxes the same two-thirds vote
requirement that already applies to special taxes referred by local governments, closing the
disparity the Upland decision opened, and the record since 2017 shows the gap it closes is not
hypothetical: roughly two dozen local special taxes have been enacted statewide by simple
majority under the current rule. Of note, the empirical research on supermajority tax rules
generally is mixed as to whether such thresholds meaningfully change tax levels, so the

treatment as agency-initiated ones — and not serve as a route to bypass the two-thirds threshold
— rather than on a confident revenue prediction.

“Upland loophole.” Separately reinforces the existing constitutional prohibition on local ad

Background
Proposition 13 (1978) capped the property tax rate at one percent of assessed value, limited
annual increases in assessed value to two percent until a change of ownership, and required a
two-thirds vote of local electorates for local special taxes — those whose revenue is legally
dedicated to a specific purpose, as distinct from general taxes that flow to a jurisdiction’s general
fund. That requirement was refined by Proposition 218 (1996). In 2017, the California Supreme
Court’s decision in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland created uncertainty about
whether the two-thirds requirement applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by citizen
initiative rather than by a local government; several lower courts subsequently upheld citizen-
initiated special taxes adopted by simple majority, opening what is commonly called the “Upland
loophole.”
The record since 2017 gives voters a concrete basis for weighing this measure rather than a
purely hypothetical one. By one count, cities and counties have enacted roughly two dozen
special-tax measures statewide by margins of less than two-thirds since Upland, including parcel,
sales, and gross-receipts taxes dedicated to schools, parks, street repairs, transit, and housing,
placed on the ballot by proponents ranging from homeless-services advocates and environmental
groups to organized labor. Los Angeles’s 2022 Measure ULA, a tax on high-value real estate
transfers, is the best-known example. Opponents of this measure have pointed to more recent
examples they say illustrate what a two-thirds requirement would foreclose going forward:
Alameda County’s November 2025 Measure B, a parcel tax supporting Washington Hospital,
passed with 64.7 percent of the vote, and Sonoma County’s March 2024 Measure H, a sales tax
funding fire and disaster response, passed with 61 percent — both comfortably above a simple
majority but short of two-thirds.
Broader research on supermajority requirements for taxation is relevant but not squarely on
point. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, reviewing states that require a legislative
supermajority to raise state taxes, has found that those states have historically levied taxes at
levels nearly identical, on average, to states without such a requirement, suggesting such rules do
not reliably reduce the level of taxation over the long run; other research reaches more favorable
conclusions for supermajority rules, and the evidence is genuinely mixed. That research,
however, examines a two-thirds vote of a legislature to raise state taxes, a different mechanism
than this measure, which asks whether voters themselves must clear a two-thirds threshold to
approve a local special tax. Direct empirical evidence on this specific mechanism is limited, in
part because the simple-majority pathway it would close has existed only since 2017.
The Proposal
Proposition 43 reached the ballot through an unusual path. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers
Association had qualified a broader citizen initiative for the November 2026 ballot that
combined a two-thirds fix for the Upland loophole with a cap on local real estate transfer taxes
SDtaxpayers.org • 3
and the retroactive voiding of existing transfer taxes above that cap, including Measure ULA. In
the closing days before the ballot was finalized, the Legislature passed this measure and
rescinded a prior “poison pill” provision in exchange for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers
Association withdrawing its broader initiative; the transfer-tax provisions were dropped in that
exchange and do not appear here.
The measure adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution. It raises no
revenue and imposes no new tax. Its principal provisions are:
● Two-thirds vote for all local special taxes: beginning January 1, 2027, no local government
— including the electorate of a local government acting through the initiative power — may
impose, extend, or increase a special tax without approval by two-thirds of those voting,
eliminating the distinction the Upland decision had opened between government-proposed
and citizen-initiated special taxes.
● Ad valorem property tax prohibition: bars any local government — and, again, the
electorate acting by initiative — from imposing a new ad valorem tax (a tax based on a
property’s value) on real property beyond what the Constitution already permits under
Article XIII A and Article XIII D. In practical terms, this forecloses using the citizen-
initiative route the Upland decision opened to enact a property tax that would sidestep
Proposition 13’s one-percent rate cap — a more direct protection of Proposition 13’s central
limit than the special-tax threshold itself.
● Prospective application only: the measure applies to special taxes imposed, extended, or
increased on or after January 1, 2027 and does not affect any existing voter-approved special
tax. Because the measure reaches the extension of a special tax, however, an existing
temporary special tax that was adopted by simple majority would face the two-thirds
threshold when it later comes up for renewal, so the measure’s practical reach extends over
time to the many local special taxes now on a fixed sunset.
The measure does not cap or otherwise affect local real estate transfer taxes, and does not
retroactively affect any existing tax. It also does not change Proposition 13's one-percent
property tax rate cap, its two-percent annual assessment-growth limit, or the property tax base
that funds schools and local services.
Taxpayers Association Findings
Fiscal Impact on Taxpayers
No official fiscal estimate specific to this measure was available to staff as of this draft.
Qualitatively, the roughly two dozen special-tax measures enacted statewide since 2017 by less
than two-thirds — including the two specific examples described above under Background,
which passed with 64.7 percent and 61 percent — give a rough sense of what is at stake: a
meaningful share of future local special taxes that would pass by simple majority would fail to
reach a two-thirds threshold, translating into foregone local revenue for the agencies that would
SDtaxpayers.org • 4
have sponsored them, relative to continuing under current law. Staff has not located an aggregate
estimate of how much revenue such measures have generated statewide to date, information the
Board may wish to request before finalizing a position.
Governance Impact
This measure presents a single central governance tradeoff. The Association’s preference is that
citizen-initiated special taxes receive the same treatment as those referred by a local government
— namely the two-thirds threshold that has applied to agency-proposed special taxes since
Proposition 13 — rather than allowing the citizen-initiative power to become a route for
approving dedicated taxes by simple majority, including taxes that fund services traditionally
supported by the general fund. Closing the Upland loophole restores that parity and advances the
principle that a dedicated tax increase should command broad consensus regardless of who
places it on the ballot. Set against that is the principle of local control and local fiscal self-
determination: the measure constrains the ability of a simple majority of local voters to tax
themselves for services they choose, whether that tax is proposed by a local government or by
citizen initiative. The record of roughly two dozen measures passed by less than two-thirds since
2017 shows this is a live, regularly exercised form of local decision-making, not a rare or
theoretical one.
Areas of Concern
The principal concern is the local-control tension described above: opponents may frame a two-
thirds requirement for citizen-initiated special taxes as a restriction on local majorities’ ability to
fund community priorities they have chosen for themselves, particularly for services such as
transit, fire protection, and homelessness response that have relied on the simple-majority
pathway in recent years.
Second, voters should understand what this measure does not reach. In its recent review of local
general-purpose sales tax measures, the Taxpayers Association has flagged a standing concern
distinct from anything at issue here: a city council places a general tax on the ballot, which
requires only a simple majority and legally dedicates the revenue to nothing, while the
accompanying campaign describes a specific list of infrastructure or service priorities the money
is said to fund. None of that is legally binding, and a future council remains free to redirect the
revenue to any lawful purpose without further voter approval. This measure does not close that
gap. It raises the vote threshold only for special taxes — those that legally dedicate revenue to a
stated purpose — and only to equalize the citizen-initiative and government-referred paths within
that category; it leaves the general-tax path, and a council’s choice to use general-tax financing
while marketing it as if it were dedicated, entirely untouched. A city that wants the simple-
majority threshold need only continue structuring its measure as a general tax.
Third, the empirical case for taxpayer savings is less certain than the policy argument for broad
consensus. Research on supermajority requirements to raise taxes is mixed, and the closest
SDtaxpayers.org • 5
available evidence concerns a different mechanism (legislative supermajorities for state tax
increases) than the one this measure proposes (voter supermajorities for local special taxes).
Voters should support or oppose this measure on the strength of the consensus-threshold
principle itself, not on an assured expectation that it will meaningfully lower local tax burdens.
Proponents
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, through proponent Jon Coupal, supports the measure
as achieving the two-thirds-threshold protection it has long sought for local special taxes.
General taxpayer and business organizations that favor a two-thirds threshold for local special
taxes, such as the California Taxpayers Association and the California Business Roundtable,
would be expected to support the measure on the same grounds, though Staff has not confirmed
formal positions. Commercial real estate and development interests that have separately
advocated for capping or eliminating local real estate transfer taxes are not understood to be
significant funders of this measure, since it does not address transfer taxes.
Opponents
Local government officials and associations and public-sector unions can be expected to oppose
raising the vote threshold for citizen-initiated special taxes, on the ground that it restricts local
voters' ability to fund local priorities by simple majority. Transit advocates, including the
organization Seamless Bay Area, have opposed the measure specifically on the ground that it
would make future transit funding measures harder to pass, citing Alameda County's Measure B
and Sonoma County's Measure H, described above, as examples of recent measures that would
not have cleared a two-thirds threshold.

Endorsement: Back Prop. 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions on local taxes
Californians have already approved these limits twice, only to have courts erode the will of the electorate

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.
