As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Local Taxes: Limitation (Proposition 43)
August 2026
TAXPAYERS ASSOCIATION POSITION SUPPORT
Rationale for Position:
Proposition 43 would extend to citizen-initiated local special taxes the same two-thirds vote
requirement that already applies to special taxes referred by local governments, closing the
disparity the Upland decision opened, and the record since 2017 shows the gap it closes is not
hypothetical: roughly two dozen local special taxes have been enacted statewide by simple
majority under the current rule. Of note, the empirical research on supermajority tax rules
generally is mixed as to whether such thresholds meaningfully change tax levels, so the
recommendation rests on the principle that citizen-initiated special taxes should receive the same
treatment as agency-initiated ones — and not serve as a route to bypass the two-thirds threshold
— rather than on a confident revenue prediction.
Title: Local taxes: limitation. Ballot designation: Proposition 43. Staff to confirm the certified
ballot title, label, and summary against the Secretary of State’s Voter Information Guide once
published.
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment
22, authored by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks; approved by a two-thirds vote of the
Legislature on June 25, 2026, and enacted as Resolution Chapter 132, Statutes of 2026); adds
Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution.
Vote: November 2026 Statewide General Election
Status: Placed on the November 2026 ballot directly by the Legislature; no citizen signature-
gathering was required or occurred.
Description: Beginning January 1, 2027, requires approval by two-thirds of the electorate
before any local government — including the electorate acting through the citizen-initiative
power — may impose, extend, or increase a special tax, closing what is commonly called the
“Upland loophole.” Separately reinforces the existing constitutional prohibition on local ad
valorem property taxes outside the framework the Constitution already permits.
Fiscal Impact: Staff has not identified an official Legislative Analyst’s Office or Department
of Finance fiscal estimate for this measure as of this draft; Staff to obtain the estimate prepared
for the Voter Information Guide once published. Because the measure applies only
prospectively to future local special taxes, any fiscal effect would take the form of foregone
local revenue relative to current law, not a change to any tax now in effect.
SDtaxpayers.org • 2
Background
Proposition 13 (1978) capped the property tax rate at one percent of assessed value, limited
annual increases in assessed value to two percent until a change of ownership, and required a
two-thirds vote of local electorates for local special taxes — those whose revenue is legally
dedicated to a specific purpose, as distinct from general taxes that flow to a jurisdiction’s general
fund. That requirement was refined by Proposition 218 (1996). In 2017, the California Supreme
Court’s decision in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland created uncertainty about
whether the two-thirds requirement applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by citizen
initiative rather than by a local government; several lower courts subsequently upheld citizen-
initiated special taxes adopted by simple majority, opening what is commonly called the “Upland
loophole.”
The record since 2017 gives voters a concrete basis for weighing this measure rather than a
purely hypothetical one. By one count, cities and counties have enacted roughly two dozen
special-tax measures statewide by margins of less than two-thirds since Upland, including parcel,
sales, and gross-receipts taxes dedicated to schools, parks, street repairs, transit, and housing,
placed on the ballot by proponents ranging from homeless-services advocates and environmental
groups to organized labor. Los Angeles’s 2022 Measure ULA, a tax on high-value real estate
transfers, is the best-known example. Opponents of this measure have pointed to more recent
examples they say illustrate what a two-thirds requirement would foreclose going forward:
Alameda County’s November 2025 Measure B, a parcel tax supporting Washington Hospital,
passed with 64.7 percent of the vote, and Sonoma County’s March 2024 Measure H, a sales tax
funding fire and disaster response, passed with 61 percent — both comfortably above a simple
majority but short of two-thirds.
Broader research on supermajority requirements for taxation is relevant but not squarely on
point. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, reviewing states that require a legislative
supermajority to raise state taxes, has found that those states have historically levied taxes at
levels nearly identical, on average, to states without such a requirement, suggesting such rules do
not reliably reduce the level of taxation over the long run; other research reaches more favorable
conclusions for supermajority rules, and the evidence is genuinely mixed. That research,
however, examines a two-thirds vote of a legislature to raise state taxes, a different mechanism
than this measure, which asks whether voters themselves must clear a two-thirds threshold to
approve a local special tax. Direct empirical evidence on this specific mechanism is limited, in
part because the simple-majority pathway it would close has existed only since 2017.
The Proposal
Proposition 43 reached the ballot through an unusual path. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers
Association had qualified a broader citizen initiative for the November 2026 ballot that
combined a two-thirds fix for the Upland loophole with a cap on local real estate transfer taxes
SDtaxpayers.org • 3
and the retroactive voiding of existing transfer taxes above that cap, including Measure ULA. In
the closing days before the ballot was finalized, the Legislature passed this measure and
rescinded a prior “poison pill” provision in exchange for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers
Association withdrawing its broader initiative; the transfer-tax provisions were dropped in that
exchange and do not appear here.
The measure adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution. It raises no
revenue and imposes no new tax. Its principal provisions are:
● Two-thirds vote for all local special taxes: beginning January 1, 2027, no local government
— including the electorate of a local government acting through the initiative power — may
impose, extend, or increase a special tax without approval by two-thirds of those voting,
eliminating the distinction the Upland decision had opened between government-proposed
and citizen-initiated special taxes.
● Ad valorem property tax prohibition: bars any local government — and, again, the
electorate acting by initiative — from imposing a new ad valorem tax (a tax based on a
property’s value) on real property beyond what the Constitution already permits under
Article XIII A and Article XIII D. In practical terms, this forecloses using the citizen-
initiative route the Upland decision opened to enact a property tax that would sidestep
Proposition 13’s one-percent rate cap — a more direct protection of Proposition 13’s central
limit than the special-tax threshold itself.
● Prospective application only: the measure applies to special taxes imposed, extended, or
increased on or after January 1, 2027 and does not affect any existing voter-approved special
tax. Because the measure reaches the extension of a special tax, however, an existing
temporary special tax that was adopted by simple majority would face the two-thirds
threshold when it later comes up for renewal, so the measure’s practical reach extends over
time to the many local special taxes now on a fixed sunset.
The measure does not cap or otherwise affect local real estate transfer taxes, and does not
retroactively affect any existing tax. It also does not change Proposition 13's one-percent
property tax rate cap, its two-percent annual assessment-growth limit, or the property tax base
that funds schools and local services.
Taxpayers Association Findings
Fiscal Impact on Taxpayers
No official fiscal estimate specific to this measure was available to staff as of this draft.
Qualitatively, the roughly two dozen special-tax measures enacted statewide since 2017 by less
than two-thirds — including the two specific examples described above under Background,
which passed with 64.7 percent and 61 percent — give a rough sense of what is at stake: a
meaningful share of future local special taxes that would pass by simple majority would fail to
reach a two-thirds threshold, translating into foregone local revenue for the agencies that would
SDtaxpayers.org • 4
have sponsored them, relative to continuing under current law. Staff has not located an aggregate
estimate of how much revenue such measures have generated statewide to date, information the
Board may wish to request before finalizing a position.
Governance Impact
This measure presents a single central governance tradeoff. The Association’s preference is that
citizen-initiated special taxes receive the same treatment as those referred by a local government
— namely the two-thirds threshold that has applied to agency-proposed special taxes since
Proposition 13 — rather than allowing the citizen-initiative power to become a route for
approving dedicated taxes by simple majority, including taxes that fund services traditionally
supported by the general fund. Closing the Upland loophole restores that parity and advances the
principle that a dedicated tax increase should command broad consensus regardless of who
places it on the ballot. Set against that is the principle of local control and local fiscal self-
determination: the measure constrains the ability of a simple majority of local voters to tax
themselves for services they choose, whether that tax is proposed by a local government or by
citizen initiative. The record of roughly two dozen measures passed by less than two-thirds since
2017 shows this is a live, regularly exercised form of local decision-making, not a rare or
theoretical one.
Areas of Concern
The principal concern is the local-control tension described above: opponents may frame a two-
thirds requirement for citizen-initiated special taxes as a restriction on local majorities’ ability to
fund community priorities they have chosen for themselves, particularly for services such as
transit, fire protection, and homelessness response that have relied on the simple-majority
pathway in recent years.
Second, voters should understand what this measure does not reach. In its recent review of local
general-purpose sales tax measures, the Taxpayers Association has flagged a standing concern
distinct from anything at issue here: a city council places a general tax on the ballot, which
requires only a simple majority and legally dedicates the revenue to nothing, while the
accompanying campaign describes a specific list of infrastructure or service priorities the money
is said to fund. None of that is legally binding, and a future council remains free to redirect the
revenue to any lawful purpose without further voter approval. This measure does not close that
gap. It raises the vote threshold only for special taxes — those that legally dedicate revenue to a
stated purpose — and only to equalize the citizen-initiative and government-referred paths within
that category; it leaves the general-tax path, and a council’s choice to use general-tax financing
while marketing it as if it were dedicated, entirely untouched. A city that wants the simple-
majority threshold need only continue structuring its measure as a general tax.
Third, the empirical case for taxpayer savings is less certain than the policy argument for broad
consensus. Research on supermajority requirements to raise taxes is mixed, and the closest
SDtaxpayers.org • 5
available evidence concerns a different mechanism (legislative supermajorities for state tax
increases) than the one this measure proposes (voter supermajorities for local special taxes).
Voters should support or oppose this measure on the strength of the consensus-threshold
principle itself, not on an assured expectation that it will meaningfully lower local tax burdens.
Proponents
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, through proponent Jon Coupal, supports the measure
as achieving the two-thirds-threshold protection it has long sought for local special taxes.
General taxpayer and business organizations that favor a two-thirds threshold for local special
taxes, such as the California Taxpayers Association and the California Business Roundtable,
would be expected to support the measure on the same grounds, though Staff has not confirmed
formal positions. Commercial real estate and development interests that have separately
advocated for capping or eliminating local real estate transfer taxes are not understood to be
significant funders of this measure, since it does not address transfer taxes.
Opponents
Local government officials and associations and public-sector unions can be expected to oppose
raising the vote threshold for citizen-initiated special taxes, on the ground that it restricts local
voters' ability to fund local priorities by simple majority. Transit advocates, including the
organization Seamless Bay Area, have opposed the measure specifically on the ground that it
would make future transit funding measures harder to pass, citing Alameda County's Measure B
and Sonoma County's Measure H, described above, as examples of recent measures that would
not have cleared a two-thirds threshold.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Don’t forget to use KQED’s voter guide (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide) when filling out your ballot!
Plus, check out Political Breakdown’s weekly newsletter (https://www.kqed.org/newsletters/political-breakdown), delivered straight to your inbox.

The truth about Prop. 43: Don’t fall for the fearmongering

By Jon Coupal (https://www.dailynews.com/author/jon-coupal/) |
PUBLISHED: October 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 4, 2026 at 5:02 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
As voting begins in this election season, it is a good time to start considering some of the more egregious lies being foisted on voters in campaign ads, editorials and op-eds.
Let’s start with what is being represented about Proposition 43, the effort to close a court-created loophole in Proposition 13. Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes and parcel taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters.
Note what Prop. 43 does not do. It does not cut any local taxes. It does not retroactively invalidate any existing tax. It does not limit any local governments from going to the voters for general tax increases, which pass with a simple majority vote. All that it does is restore the two-thirds vote for local special taxes – taxes imposed for a specific purpose.
Despite the negligible impact Prop. 43 would have on existing local government revenues, according to critics, Prop. 43 will result in the end of civilization. In an op-ed in the San Jose Mercury News, the president of California Professional Firefighters, Darrell Roberts, claims that Prop. 43 “would place a nearly insurmountable roadblock from placing any measure on the ballot” to impose a special tax. What Mr. Roberts forgets is that the two-thirds vote for local special taxes was a provision of the California Constitution from 1978 until 2017 when the California courts began crafting an exception. During that time, rather than being an “insurmountable” barrier, special taxes were routinely enacted with the requisite two-thirds vote, including sales taxes and parcel taxes.
The argument that supermajority vote requirements are somehow “undemocratic” collapses when one considers the long history of America’s constitutional framework. There are no fewer than twelve instances in the U.S. Constitution requiring a two-thirds vote. These include impeachment; expelling a Member of Congress; overriding a veto; amending the Constitution (Congressional approval of a Joint Resolution proposing an amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires a 2/3 majority); calling a Constitutional Convention; and ratifying a treaty.
Here in California, the two-thirds vote requirement on matters related to taxation dates back to 1879. That was when the higher threshold was placed in the state constitution for local general obligation bonds as a protection against excessive debt at the local level, repaid by property owners. Recently, in the November 2024 election, California voters overwhelmingly rejected an effort to lower the two-thirds vote requirement for most local bonds to 55%. Prop. 5 lost by ten points.
What is revealing about the opposition to Prop. 43 is that most is coming from public sector labor organizations – the very interests who want to remove all barriers to higher taxes.
Hyperbolic support for tax increases is prevalent throughout the local level of government as well. Although not a statewide measure, a proposal to raise the sales taxes in five Bay Area counties to generate billions for failed transit systems has driven proponents of the tax to near madness in describing the parade of horribles if the tax fails in November. But this “Regional Transit Measure” has weak support notwithstanding a well-funded campaign to promote it. Voters are suspicious because the transit districts in question, especially BART, have done nothing to correct their failures and inefficiencies. Not surprisingly, Bay Area residents want at least some proof that the new revenue won’t be as misspent as existing revenue.

Despite the track record of waste and fraud, major Bay Area media outlets are fully in support of increasing sales taxes, which everyone admits are very regressive. The San Francisco Chronicle warns that, “without an immediate infusion of funds, Muni could be forced to cut service by at least 30%, cancel at least 20 bus routes, end regular evening service, eliminate cable car service and reduce fare discounts for vulnerable populations. BART could close 15 stations and reduce service by 70%. Caltrain could reduce service to one train per hour and stop service on weekends.”
The organization Fixes Before Funding disputes these dire predictions, noting, “Transit costs and subsidies have exploded while service shrank; when ridership and fare revenue collapsed, the agencies did not restructure; spending per rider has gone off the chart; ridership never recovered, and never grew the way planners promised; and, the signature projects ran over budget and under-delivered.”
A great deal of overstatement can be expected in any political contest, but when it comes to the predictions of disaster if more taxes are not forthcoming, voters would be well advised to ignore the hype.
Jon Coupal is president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

By Jon Coupal (https://www.dailynews.com/author/jon-coupal/) |
PUBLISHED: October 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 4, 2026 at 5:02 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
As voting begins in this election season, it is a good time to start considering some of the more egregious lies being foisted on voters in campaign ads, editorials and op-eds.
Let’s start with what is being represented about Proposition 43, the effort to close a court-created loophole in Proposition 13. Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes and parcel taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters.
Note what Prop. 43 does not do. It does not cut any local taxes. It does not retroactively invalidate any existing tax. It does not limit any local governments from going to the voters for general tax increases, which pass with a simple majority vote. All that it does is restore the two-thirds vote for local special taxes – taxes imposed for a specific purpose.
Despite the negligible impact Prop. 43 would have on existing local government revenues, according to critics, Prop. 43 will result in the end of civilization. In an op-ed in the San Jose Mercury News, the president of California Professional Firefighters, Darrell Roberts, claims that Prop. 43 “would place a nearly insurmountable roadblock from placing any measure on the ballot” to impose a special tax. What Mr. Roberts forgets is that the two-thirds vote for local special taxes was a provision of the California Constitution from 1978 until 2017 when the California courts began crafting an exception. During that time, rather than being an “insurmountable” barrier, special taxes were routinely enacted with the requisite two-thirds vote, including sales taxes and parcel taxes.
The argument that supermajority vote requirements are somehow “undemocratic” collapses when one considers the long history of America’s constitutional framework. There are no fewer than twelve instances in the U.S. Constitution requiring a two-thirds vote. These include impeachment; expelling a Member of Congress; overriding a veto; amending the Constitution (Congressional approval of a Joint Resolution proposing an amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires a 2/3 majority); calling a Constitutional Convention; and ratifying a treaty.
Here in California, the two-thirds vote requirement on matters related to taxation dates back to 1879. That was when the higher threshold was placed in the state constitution for local general obligation bonds as a protection against excessive debt at the local level, repaid by property owners. Recently, in the November 2024 election, California voters overwhelmingly rejected an effort to lower the two-thirds vote requirement for most local bonds to 55%. Prop. 5 lost by ten points.
What is revealing about the opposition to Prop. 43 is that most is coming from public sector labor organizations – the very interests who want to remove all barriers to higher taxes.
Hyperbolic support for tax increases is prevalent throughout the local level of government as well. Although not a statewide measure, a proposal to raise the sales taxes in five Bay Area counties to generate billions for failed transit systems has driven proponents of the tax to near madness in describing the parade of horribles if the tax fails in November. But this “Regional Transit Measure” has weak support notwithstanding a well-funded campaign to promote it. Voters are suspicious because the transit districts in question, especially BART, have done nothing to correct their failures and inefficiencies. Not surprisingly, Bay Area residents want at least some proof that the new revenue won’t be as misspent as existing revenue.

Despite the track record of waste and fraud, major Bay Area media outlets are fully in support of increasing sales taxes, which everyone admits are very regressive. The San Francisco Chronicle warns that, “without an immediate infusion of funds, Muni could be forced to cut service by at least 30%, cancel at least 20 bus routes, end regular evening service, eliminate cable car service and reduce fare discounts for vulnerable populations. BART could close 15 stations and reduce service by 70%. Caltrain could reduce service to one train per hour and stop service on weekends.”
The organization Fixes Before Funding disputes these dire predictions, noting, “Transit costs and subsidies have exploded while service shrank; when ridership and fare revenue collapsed, the agencies did not restructure; spending per rider has gone off the chart; ridership never recovered, and never grew the way planners promised; and, the signature projects ran over budget and under-delivered.”
A great deal of overstatement can be expected in any political contest, but when it comes to the predictions of disaster if more taxes are not forthcoming, voters would be well advised to ignore the hype.

By Jon Coupal (https://www.dailynews.com/author/jon-coupal/) |
PUBLISHED: October 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 4, 2026 at 5:02 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
As voting begins in this election season, it is a good time to start considering some of the more egregious lies being foisted on voters in campaign ads, editorials and op-eds.
Let’s start with what is being represented about Proposition 43, the effort to close a court-created loophole in Proposition 13. Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes and parcel taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters.
Note what Prop. 43 does not do. It does not cut any local taxes. It does not retroactively invalidate any existing tax. It does not limit any local governments from going to the voters for general tax increases, which pass with a simple majority vote. All that it does is restore the two-thirds vote for local special taxes – taxes imposed for a specific purpose.
Despite the negligible impact Prop. 43 would have on existing local government revenues, according to critics, Prop. 43 will result in the end of civilization. In an op-ed in the San Jose Mercury News, the president of California Professional Firefighters, Darrell Roberts, claims that Prop. 43 “would place a nearly insurmountable roadblock from placing any measure on the ballot” to impose a special tax. What Mr. Roberts forgets is that the two-thirds vote for local special taxes was a provision of the California Constitution from 1978 until 2017 when the California courts began crafting an exception. During that time, rather than being an “insurmountable” barrier, special taxes were routinely enacted with the requisite two-thirds vote, including sales taxes and parcel taxes.
The argument that supermajority vote requirements are somehow “undemocratic” collapses when one considers the long history of America’s constitutional framework. There are no fewer than twelve instances in the U.S. Constitution requiring a two-thirds vote. These include impeachment; expelling a Member of Congress; overriding a veto; amending the Constitution (Congressional approval of a Joint Resolution proposing an amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires a 2/3 majority); calling a Constitutional Convention; and ratifying a treaty.
Here in California, the two-thirds vote requirement on matters related to taxation dates back to 1879. That was when the higher threshold was placed in the state constitution for local general obligation bonds as a protection against excessive debt at the local level, repaid by property owners. Recently, in the November 2024 election, California voters overwhelmingly rejected an effort to lower the two-thirds vote requirement for most local bonds to 55%. Prop. 5 lost by ten points.
What is revealing about the opposition to Prop. 43 is that most is coming from public sector labor organizations – the very interests who want to remove all barriers to higher taxes.
Hyperbolic support for tax increases is prevalent throughout the local level of government as well. Although not a statewide measure, a proposal to raise the sales taxes in five Bay Area counties to generate billions for failed transit systems has driven proponents of the tax to near madness in describing the parade of horribles if the tax fails in November. But this “Regional Transit Measure” has weak support notwithstanding a well-funded campaign to promote it. Voters are suspicious because the transit districts in question, especially BART, have done nothing to correct their failures and inefficiencies. Not surprisingly, Bay Area residents want at least some proof that the new revenue won’t be as misspent as existing revenue.

Despite the track record of waste and fraud, major Bay Area media outlets are fully in support of increasing sales taxes, which everyone admits are very regressive. The San Francisco Chronicle warns that, “without an immediate infusion of funds, Muni could be forced to cut service by at least 30%, cancel at least 20 bus routes, end regular evening service, eliminate cable car service and reduce fare discounts for vulnerable populations. BART could close 15 stations and reduce service by 70%. Caltrain could reduce service to one train per hour and stop service on weekends.”
The organization Fixes Before Funding disputes these dire predictions, noting, “Transit costs and subsidies have exploded while service shrank; when ridership and fare revenue collapsed, the agencies did not restructure; spending per rider has gone off the chart; ridership never recovered, and never grew the way planners promised; and, the signature projects ran over budget and under-delivered.”
A great deal of overstatement can be expected in any political contest, but when it comes to the predictions of disaster if more taxes are not forthcoming, voters would be well advised to ignore the hype.

I think I already have enough, but I want to double-check the Placer County and transit sales tax situation, since Prop 43 requires a two-thirds vote to extend special taxes, which would cover existing citizen-initiated taxes with sunsets.

I'm confirming the extension point with the LAO, which states that any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote, so existing sunset taxes would be covered. Next I'll check the KQED piece on opponents' claims for any nuance, especially whether the Bay Area transit measure on this ballot is affected.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

By Jon Coupal (https://www.dailynews.com/author/jon-coupal/) |
PUBLISHED: October 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 4, 2026 at 5:02 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
As voting begins in this election season, it is a good time to start considering some of the more egregious lies being foisted on voters in campaign ads, editorials and op-eds.
Let’s start with what is being represented about Proposition 43, the effort to close a court-created loophole in Proposition 13. Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes and parcel taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters.
Note what Prop. 43 does not do. It does not cut any local taxes. It does not retroactively invalidate any existing tax. It does not limit any local governments from going to the voters for general tax increases, which pass with a simple majority vote. All that it does is restore the two-thirds vote for local special taxes – taxes imposed for a specific purpose.
Despite the negligible impact Prop. 43 would have on existing local government revenues, according to critics, Prop. 43 will result in the end of civilization. In an op-ed in the San Jose Mercury News, the president of California Professional Firefighters, Darrell Roberts, claims that Prop. 43 “would place a nearly insurmountable roadblock from placing any measure on the ballot” to impose a special tax. What Mr. Roberts forgets is that the two-thirds vote for local special taxes was a provision of the California Constitution from 1978 until 2017 when the California courts began crafting an exception. During that time, rather than being an “insurmountable” barrier, special taxes were routinely enacted with the requisite two-thirds vote, including sales taxes and parcel taxes.
The argument that supermajority vote requirements are somehow “undemocratic” collapses when one considers the long history of America’s constitutional framework. There are no fewer than twelve instances in the U.S. Constitution requiring a two-thirds vote. These include impeachment; expelling a Member of Congress; overriding a veto; amending the Constitution (Congressional approval of a Joint Resolution proposing an amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires a 2/3 majority); calling a Constitutional Convention; and ratifying a treaty.
Here in California, the two-thirds vote requirement on matters related to taxation dates back to 1879. That was when the higher threshold was placed in the state constitution for local general obligation bonds as a protection against excessive debt at the local level, repaid by property owners. Recently, in the November 2024 election, California voters overwhelmingly rejected an effort to lower the two-thirds vote requirement for most local bonds to 55%. Prop. 5 lost by ten points.
What is revealing about the opposition to Prop. 43 is that most is coming from public sector labor organizations – the very interests who want to remove all barriers to higher taxes.
Hyperbolic support for tax increases is prevalent throughout the local level of government as well. Although not a statewide measure, a proposal to raise the sales taxes in five Bay Area counties to generate billions for failed transit systems has driven proponents of the tax to near madness in describing the parade of horribles if the tax fails in November. But this “Regional Transit Measure” has weak support notwithstanding a well-funded campaign to promote it. Voters are suspicious because the transit districts in question, especially BART, have done nothing to correct their failures and inefficiencies. Not surprisingly, Bay Area residents want at least some proof that the new revenue won’t be as misspent as existing revenue.

Despite the track record of waste and fraud, major Bay Area media outlets are fully in support of increasing sales taxes, which everyone admits are very regressive. The San Francisco Chronicle warns that, “without an immediate infusion of funds, Muni could be forced to cut service by at least 30%, cancel at least 20 bus routes, end regular evening service, eliminate cable car service and reduce fare discounts for vulnerable populations. BART could close 15 stations and reduce service by 70%. Caltrain could reduce service to one train per hour and stop service on weekends.”
The organization Fixes Before Funding disputes these dire predictions, noting, “Transit costs and subsidies have exploded while service shrank; when ridership and fare revenue collapsed, the agencies did not restructure; spending per rider has gone off the chart; ridership never recovered, and never grew the way planners promised; and, the signature projects ran over budget and under-delivered.”
A great deal of overstatement can be expected in any political contest, but when it comes to the predictions of disaster if more taxes are not forthcoming, voters would be well advised to ignore the hype.

Now I'm weighing the last point: some pro-43 taxpayer groups concede the measure could push local governments toward general taxes, which need only a majority and carry no legal earmark. Opponents' warnings about blocking fire and police funding also go further than the text does, since general taxes still pass by simple majority.

Now I'm settling on the shape of the answer: I won't give a one-word pick, since this comes down to how much weight to give majority rule versus a harder bar for earmarked taxes, and that's a values call for the voter.

Now I'm checking the specifics against the wording of the measure: the two-thirds rule would hit citizen-initiated special taxes, and renewals of those would need it too.

Now I'm checking the lean-no points: the case that a local majority should keep the power to tax itself for fire, transit, or housing, and the concern that a third of voters can block a measure most people back, which would have sunk taxes that drew 55 to 65 percent support, like LA's mansion tax and Sonoma's fire tax. Then I'm listing who backs each side, starting with the Yes camp: the Howard Jarvis group, CalTax, CalChamber, the state GOP, and several newspaper boards, including the Mercury News and the San Diego Union-

Now I'm checking the Sonoma fire tax detail, since I want to confirm whether it was citizen-initiated before I cite it as an example of a measure that would have failed under this rule.

Now I'm checking the Sonoma figure against the sources: a county councilmember and the San Diego Taxpayers group both describe Measure H as passing in 2024 with about 61 percent, so the counterfactual holds, even though the existing tax stays in place.

Now I'm verifying the No side's claim that Prop 43 makes it easier for corporate interests to dodge taxes. That's the one line I haven't checked against the measure's text yet.

Now I'm weighing whether the No side's warnings hold up as well. Their claim that the measure blocks fire and police funding is overstated, since general taxes still pass by simple majority, so I'll note that alongside the Yes side's overreach.

I'm working out how to present what Prop 43 actually does. Both campaigns overstate things: the Yes side's spending safeguards aren't in the text, since special taxes are already limited to their stated purpose, and the No side's fire-and-police warnings only apply to earmarked taxes, because general taxes still pass by simple majority. Now I'm starting the breakdown with the 2027 change to citizen-petition special taxes.

Now I'm going over the remaining points: Prop 43 doesn't repeal any existing tax, and renewing a citizen-passed special tax would also need two-thirds, while general taxes still pass by simple majority. Both campaigns overstate something, since the Yes side's spending safeguards are already law for special taxes and the No side's fire-and-police warnings only cover earmarked taxes. I'm also noting that the near-unanimous legislative vote was a deal to take a broader Howard Jarvis initiative off the ballot, and even the measure's author, Buffy Wicks, is urging a No vote.

Now I'm settling the wording on the No side's claims: the fire-and-police warnings only reach citizen-proposed earmarked taxes, since government-placed special taxes already need two-thirds. So Prop 43 really only changes the citizen-initiated case, and I'll say that precisely.

I'm settling on not giving a single verdict and instead laying out the key facts and how each side overstates, so the decision stays with the voter.

I'm not going to give you a one-word answer on this one. After researching it, I don't think there's an objectively "better" vote. It comes down to how you weigh majority rule against making taxes harder to raise, and that's your call. Here's the short version.

**What Prop 43 actually does**
- Starting in 2027, a local tax earmarked for a specific purpose (a "special tax") would need two-thirds of the vote if citizens put it on the ballot by petition. Today it needs a simple majority. Special taxes put on the ballot by cities and counties already need two-thirds.
- It doesn't repeal any existing tax. Renewing an existing citizen-passed special tax would need two-thirds, though. General taxes, which aren't earmarked, still pass with a simple majority.
- Both campaigns overstate things. The Yes side suggests Prop 43 adds new rules on how the money gets spent, but special taxes are already legally limited to their stated purpose. The No side's warnings about fire and police funding only apply to earmarked taxes proposed by citizens.
- Lawmakers voted for it almost unanimously as part of a deal to get a broader Howard Jarvis initiative off the ballot. Even its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, is urging a No vote.

**Lean YES if you think:**
- The same two-thirds bar should apply no matter who puts a special tax on the ballot.
- Interest groups use petition drives to get around Prop 13's two-thirds rule.
- Earmarked tax increases should need broad agreement.

**Lean NO if you think:**
- A local majority should be able to tax itself for things like fire protection, transit or housing.
- It's wrong that about a third of voters could block a tax most people support. Taxes that passed with 55–65% of the vote, like LA's "mansion tax" and Sonoma County's fire tax, would have failed under this rule.

**Who's on each side**
- **Yes:** Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, CalTax, CalChamber, the California Republican Party, and the editorial boards of the Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune and OC Register.
- **No:** Gov. Newsom, the California Democratic Party, unions for firefighters, teachers and nurses, the League of California Cities, the League of Women Voters, SPUR, and the Sacramento Bee editorial board.

If you tell me which of those priorities matters most to you, I'll tell you which vote matches it.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
We all want relief from California’s high cost of living. But Proposition 43 doesn’t cut your taxes a penny. It attacks something far more valuable: the power of your vote.
PROP. 43 WEAKENS YOUR VOTE.
Today, when local voters decide how to fund their communities, the majority rules. Prop. 43 throws that out, letting just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Under Prop. 43, a NO vote counts twice as much as a YES. That isn’t fair, and it isn’t democracy.
PROP. 43 DEEPENS THE HOUSING CRISIS.
Across California, communities vote to build affordable homes for working families, seniors, and veterans. They are helping renters stay housed and move people off the streets. Prop. 43 hands a small minority the power to block those solutions, even when a clear majority of your neighbors support them.
PROP. 43 TIES YOUR COMMUNITY’S HANDS.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund the critical local services your community counts on: staffing fire stations and 911 response, preparing neighborhoods for wildfire, repairing crumbling roads, keeping schools, parks, and libraries open, and protecting local hospitals and clinics as Washington cuts healthcare funding. When funding is blocked, help arrives slower, classrooms grow more crowded, and communities are left less safe.
KEEP THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS-WITH YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBORS.
That’s why teachers, nurses, firefighters, and housing advocates all oppose Prop. 43.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Nick Lapis , Director of Advocacy
Californians Against Waste
Bill Barnes , Director of Campaigns & Community
Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California
Steve Frisch , President
Sierra Business Council
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 43
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts. Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions-and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.
Local police and firefighters can’t rely on Sacramento or Washington politicians. These services are funded at the local level. Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. Without adequate funding, 911 response times are slower, fire stations sit understaffed, and families wait longer for help when every second counts. When a house fire breaks out-or a wildfire threatens our neighborhoods-that local funding is what protects us. Prop. 43 would let a small minority of voters block it. Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.
Across California, local voters have come together to repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local hospitals and healthcare-especially as Washington cuts federal health funding. These are decisions communities make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43 hands a small group of voters the power to veto those solutions, even when the majority supports them.
PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY.
In America, we believe in one person, one vote-and the majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want. It puts the out-voted minority in charge-even if they are extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote.
CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.
Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold these corporations and developers accountable at the ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away-to protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.
That’s why these organizations are asking you to vote NO on Prop. 43:
• California Professional Firefighters • Californians Against Waste • California Federation of Teachers • California School Employees Association • Communities for a Better Environment • AAPI Force • Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California • Nurses Alliance of SEIU California • Sierra Business Council
Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the power where it belongs-with you and your neighbors.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Harkins , Executive Director
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Adam Weinberger , President
California School Employees Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire, local politicians waste your money on their pet projects- then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the most important priorities.
The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions in taxes they should not have had to pay.
Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas, and real estate taxes.
Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on new or higher local taxes and requires governments to spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters approved-preventing bait-and-switch schemes that make our sky-high cost of living even worse.
Over the last decade, local governments have imposed 2,000 new or higher taxes. Prop. 43 CLOSES LOOPHOLES used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases, restores the protections voters originally approved under Proposition 13, and makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes without broad voter support.
The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot sends a clear message: activist courts exceeded voters’ intent by creating loopholes that weakened Proposition 13’s protections.
Restore your right to vote on ALL local taxes.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Greg Van Dyke , Chairman
California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and
Safety

PROPOSITION 43
This amendment proposed by Assembly Constitutional
Amendment 22 of the 2025–2026 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 132, Statutes of 2026) expressly
amends the California Constitution by adding a section
thereto; therefore, new provisions proposed to be
added are printed in italic type to indicate that they are
new.
PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO ARTICLE XIII A
That Section 4.5 is added to Article XIII A thereof, to
read:
SEC. 4.5. (a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and
notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local
government, including the electorate of a local
government exercising the initiative power, may impose,
extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided
in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of
Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of
Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is
submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-
thirds vote.
(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local
government, including the electorate of a local
government exercising the initiative power, may impose
ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in
paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article
XIII D.
(c) “Local government” and “special tax” shall have the
same meaning as provided in Section 1 of Article XIII C.
PROPOSITION 44
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds sections to the
Corporations Code, Government Code, and the Health
and Safety Code; therefore, new provisions proposed to
be added are printed in italic type to indicate that they
are new.
PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Title.
This measure shall be known and may be cited as the
“Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.”
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
The people of the State of California find and declare all
of the following:
(a) Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) are a
form of community clinic that are fundamental to the
California health care safety net, as their mission is to
provide primary and preventive care to low-income and
underserved populations.
(b) Most FQHCs in the state are operated by nonprofit
organizations governed by a board whose responsibility
is to ensure that the clinic meets its missions as a
safety-net health care provider and nonprofit public
benefit corporation subject to state and federal tax
exemptions.
(c) Clinic boards have significant responsibility and
exercise a great deal of authority in decisions on both
organization design and compensation, including that
of the Chief Executive Officer and other executives.
(d) Though existing state law requires nonprofit boards
of directors to review and approve Chief Executive
Officer and Chief Financial Officer compensation to
ensure that it is just and reasonable, many clinics pay
excessive shares of their revenue towards executive
compensation, resulting in underinvestment in core
patient services.
(e) Since 2018, all nonprofits, including clinics, have
been required to report the dollar amount of their
mission-related, i.e., “program,” expenses, as well as
“management and administrative” expenses to the IRS
annually. Many clinics in California incur management
and administrative expenses that are much higher than
average—sometimes 30 to 40 percent of total
revenue—while others spend less than 10 percent.
(f) Many clinics are highly profitable, sometimes
reporting annual surpluses of as much as 20 percent of
total revenue, rather than spending the funds in a
manner consistent with their charitable mission.
(g) Worker training, recruitment, and retention are
problems for California clinics. Clinic workers report
chronic understaffing, high workloads, and staffing
turnover, as well as long wait times for patients.
(h) It is the intent of this initiative to create a
reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed
spending as a proportion of total revenue to ensure
clinic patient service delivery and workforce stability is
prioritized over management and overhead spending.
SEC. 3. Reporting Requirement.
SEC. 3.1. Section 12586.3 is added to the
Government Code, to read:
12586.3. (a) For purposes of this section, the
following definitions apply:
(1) “Clinic” means any clinic corporation, as defined at
paragraph (3) of subdivision (b) of Section 1200 of the
Health and Safety Code, that is a federally qualified
health center (FQHC) as that term is defined in Section
1396d of Title 42 of the United States Code. For
purposes of this paragraph, FQHCs include
organizations that do not receive an FQHC award, but

LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. 43
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California.
California has many local governments.
These include cities, counties, special
districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.
The State Constitution allows local
governments to increase taxes with
local voter approval. Tax increases can
be put on a ballot by voters or a local
governing board (such as a city council
or board of supervisors). Increases
in some types of local taxes require a
two-thirds vote to approve them, while
other types of taxes require a majority
(more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved
permanently, while others are
approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can
be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive
Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under
current law, local taxes that are
used for a specific purpose require a
two-thirds vote to be approved. These
are called special taxes. However,
recent court decisions have allowed
C O N T I N U E D
special taxes that are proposed by
voters to be approved with a majority
vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning
on January 1, 2027, any new,
increased, or extended local special
taxes proposed by voters would require
a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government
Tax Revenues in the Future.
Proposition 43 makes it harder for local
governments to pass certain taxes. As a
result, local governments’ tax revenues
could be lower in the future than
they otherwise would be. The actual
revenue impact is unknown and would
depend on future decisions by local
governments and voters.
Visit sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-
resources/measure-contributions/2026-
ballot-measure-contribution-totals for a list
of committees primarily formed to support or
oppose this measure.
Visit fppc.ca.gov/transparency/
top-contributors.html
to access the committee’s top 10 contributors. 43

yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately
needed local services.

SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.
Across California, local voters have come together to
repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to
fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local
hospitals and healthcare—especially as Washington cuts
federal health funding. These are decisions communities
make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43
hands a small group of voters the power to veto those
solutions, even when the majority supports them.
PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE
WILL OF THE MAJORITY.
In America, we believe in one person, one vote—and the
majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just
over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want.
It puts the out-voted minority in charge—even if they are
extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as
a YES vote.
CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.
Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in
elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold
these corporations and developers accountable at the
ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local
needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away—to
protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.
That’s why these organizations are asking you to vote NO
on Prop. 43:

Waste • California Federation of Teachers • California
School Employees Association • Communities for a
Better Environment • AAPI Force • Non-Profit Housing
Association of Northern California • Nurses Alliance of
SEIU California • Sierra Business Council
Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the
power where it belongs—with you and your neighbors.

Darrell Roberts, President

Chris Harkins, Executive Director

VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER
PROTECTIONS
Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of
prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire,
local politicians waste your money on their pet projects—
then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the
most important priorities.
The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for
taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court
decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to
pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions
in taxes they should not have had to pay.
Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds
vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting
homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly
new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas,
and real estate taxes.
Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on
new or higher local taxes and requires governments to
spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters
approved—preventing bait-and-switch schemes that
make our sky-high cost of living even worse.
Over the last decade, local governments have imposed

used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases,
restores the protections voters originally approved under

raise taxes without broad voter support.
The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place

Under Proposition 13, a local special tax, meaning one earmarked for a specific purpose, needs two-thirds of voters to pass.
City councils, county boards and special districts all live with that rule.
Then came 2017.
In *California Cannabis Coalition v.
City of Upland*, the state Supreme Court ruled on a narrow question about election timing for citizen initiatives.
Lower courts read the decision more broadly.
The result: Special taxes placed on the ballot by petition could pass with 50% plus one.
Fresno saw it play out.
Measure P, the 2018 parks sales tax, drew 52.17% of the vote.
The city treated it as defeated, and a Fresno County judge agreed.
An appeals court reversed that ruling and held that a simple majority was enough.
Proposition 43 closes that gap.
Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, any new, increased or extended local special tax proposed by voters would need two-thirds approval.
That is the same bar local governments already clear.
What it does not do:
- **Repeal any tax already on the books.**
...

-
- **Cap real estate transfer taxes.**
...
That last item was part of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s original initiative.
It was dropped in a June deal with the governor’s office and legislative leaders.
Lawmakers placed the narrower compromise, ACA 22, on the ballot by votes of 35-1 in the Senate and 68-2 in the Assembly.
