I'm weighing whether to recommend a yes or no vote on this ballot measure, which is a contested political question, so I'm thinking about how to handle a request for a one-word verdict on it.

I'm weighing whether a ballot measure on vote thresholds and local taxes is a hot-button issue where I should hold back, or whether it's more of a values-based policy question. It's less charged than something like abortion, though taxes still make it partly partisan, and the near-unanimous legislative support for the compromise is worth noting.

I'm weighing whether to give a one-word yes or no on this measure, and whether a choice here is better handled by laying out the tradeoffs than by picking a side. The near-unanimous legislative vote is partly a product of a deal to head off a worse initiative, so it may not reflect real agreement on the merits.

I'm weighing whether to give a one-word yes or no on this ballot measure, which is a contested values question about majority rule versus protection against tax increases. Balanced information is the norm for questions like this, so I'm leaning toward laying out the considerations rather than picking a side.

I'm weighing whether to answer a contested ballot question with a bare yes or no, given that an AI nudging many voters toward one side could have outsized influence on the outcome. That concern pulls me toward holding back a verdict and laying out the tradeoffs instead.

I'm considering the arguments for a yes vote: it would restore consistency, since special taxes would need a two-thirds vote whether the government or citizens place them, closing a loophole where groups use signature drives to get around that requirement. It would also match the original intent of Prop 13 and Prop 218.

I'm noting the case for yes: it would be non-retroactive, so it wouldn't repeal existing taxes, and the compromise headed off a much broader measure that could have cut up to $2 billion a year. I'm also weighing the case for no, which rests on majority rule, since a two-thirds threshold lets roughly a third of voters block a measure, and on the difficulty it creates for funding local services.

I'm weighing the arguments on the other side too: citizen initiatives are a form of direct democracy, and supermajority requirements are often criticized as anti-majoritarian because they favor the status quo. I'm also recalling a few local tax measures that passed by comfortable margins under simple-majority rules, which bears on how a higher threshold would have played out.

I'm checking how the editorial boards and Governor Newsom have weighed in on the measure, since the coalitions on each side include firefighters, teachers, and housing advocates on one and business and taxpayer groups on the other.

I'm checking whether the Democratic Party has taken a position, since I'd guess it leans No and the Republican side leans Yes, but I want to confirm that. The main question is whether I should give a one-word answer at all, and I'm weighing that against my commitment to political even-handedness on contested questions like this one.

I'm reminded that as an AI talking with many people, I should be careful not to push a whole electorate toward one side of a contested tax measure, and that professional reticence fits here, since this is a partisan tax question rather than something with an obvious answer. Even so, I can see why someone who wants a recommendation would be frustrated by a refusal to pick one.

Even so, I'm weighing whether it's right to skip the one-word verdict, since a bare recommendation on a contested tax measure would be shaping a vote on values, not facts. A short decision guide, saying what a yes or no vote prioritizes, seems more useful and leaves the choice with the user.

I'm reconsidering whether there's any version of "better" here that doesn't depend on values, like a measure with drafting flaws both sides would criticize. This one has real effects that turn on how people weigh taxes against majority rule, so a bare verdict wouldn't be fair. I'm planning to research the deal details, the LAO's analysis, editorial endorsements, and party positions before writing a balanced summary.

I'm now looking at how citizen-initiated special taxes have fared since Upland, including how many passed below two-thirds and how much revenue they raised. Bluesky (https://sdvoice.info/on-your-november-ballot-proposition-43/) Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland), author of Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 (ACA 22), which qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 43. Credit: CBM photo by Antonio Ray Harvey. By Antonio Ray Harvey , California Black Media California voters will decide this November whether to make it more difficult to approve local special taxes proposed through the citizen initiative process. Proposition (Prop) 43 would amend the California Constitution to require two-thirds voter approval for all local special taxes, including those placed on the ballot by citizens. Special taxes generate revenue dedicated to specific purposes, such as affordable housing, public transit, libraries, parks, emergency response and infrastructure. The measure has sparked debate over taxpayer protections, majority rule and the ability of local communities to generate revenue for public services. A “yes” vote would establish the two-thirds requirement beginning Jan. 1, 2027. A “no” vote would preserve current law, under which citizen-proposed local special taxes generally may pass with a simple majority. Articles like this one can be in your Inbox Be the first to know about breaking news, articles, and updates. Hot Off the Press: Thursday e-Edition Keep up to date with our print and e-digital paper editions! Newsbytes: Twice weekly updates Get news updates directly to your inbox with news that matters to you! Sign up Prop 43 originated as Assembly Constitutional Amendment (ACA) 22, authored by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland). The Legislature approved the measure June 25 by votes of 68-2 in the Assembly and 35-1 in the Senate, placing it on the ballot without requiring the governor’s signature. The measure emerged from an eleventh-hour compromise reached before the ballot certification deadline between legislative leaders and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA). Under the agreement, HJTA withdrew a broader tax-limitation initiative from the November ballot in exchange for lawmakers placing ACA 22 before voters. Legislative leaders also withdrew ACA 13, a competing constitutional amendment that would have changed the approval requirements for future voter initiatives. Under existing law, special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments already require two-thirds voter approval. However, court decisions stemming from the California Supreme Court’s 2017 ruling in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland established that the same threshold does not necessarily apply to taxes proposed by citizens. Subsequent appellate court decisions held that citizen-initiated special taxes could be approved by a simple majority. Prop 43 would eliminate that distinction by applying the two-thirds threshold to local governments and citizens exercising their initiative power. Supporters say the measure would close a legal loophole and ensure that all special taxes face the same voter-approval standard, regardless of who places them on the ballot. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA), Reform California and several taxpayer and business organizations support the measure. HJTA President Jon Coupal described its advancement as a victory for Proposition 13’s taxpayer protections. “It’s a tremendous turnaround,” Coupal said. “In 2024, the California Legislature sought to make it easier to raise taxes with Proposition 5, which the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association defeated at the ballot. [On June 25], the Legislature voted to make it harder to raise taxes by advancing a constitutional amendment, ACA 22, to close a loophole that had allowed some special taxes to pass with less than the two-thirds vote required by Proposition 13.” Sen. Tony Strickland (R-Huntington Beach) also praised the agreement, arguing that Californians need stronger protections against tax increases. “I stand with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association in defending Proposition 13 and the protections it provides for taxpayers and homeowners,” Strickland said. “Californians deserve the certainty of knowing these constitutional protections will remain in place.” Opponents argue that the measure would give a minority of voters the power to block revenue proposals supported by most residents. They contend that the higher threshold could hinder future efforts to fund affordable housing, healthcare, fire protection, public transportation and other locally determined priorities. Opponents include Wicks, despite her authorship of ACA 22, and public-service and transportation advocates, including Seamless Bay Area. Wicks said she introduced the amendment as part of a compromise to persuade HJTA to withdraw a broader tax-limitation initiative from the ballot. “I’m the author of ACA 22. I’m also adamantly opposed to it,” Wicks posted on Bluesky on June 29. “That deserves an explanation — so I want to tell you what went down [with] the ACA, and the fight over transfer taxes and the Taxpayer Protection Act.” The withdrawn initiative would have imposed additional restrictions, including limits on certain real estate transfer taxes and provisions affecting previously approved taxes. Legislative leaders also withdrew ACA 13, a competing constitutional amendment that would have applied heightened approval requirements to some future ballot initiatives. Wicks said the compromise prevented the broader proposal from reaching voters but left them with a narrower measure she still considers harmful. “I authored ACA 22 not because I wanted it to become law — but because it was the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot before time ran out,” she said. Wicks has said she viewed the compromise as choosing what she believed was the less harmful of two options, even though she ultimately opposes Proposition 43. Seamless Bay Area argues that Prop 43 could impede future local efforts to fund transit, affordable housing and other public investments. The organization points to previously approved measures supporting healthcare, fire protection and open-space preservation that received majority support but fell short of two-thirds. The California Democratic Party announced on Aug. 2 that it voted to oppose Prop 43 at its Summer Executive Board Meeting held in San Diego. The debate over Prop 43 centers on whether special taxes should require a broad public consensus or whether a simple majority should retain the authority to approve locally proposed investments. UNDER THE DOME: THE INSIDE STORY ON THE DEAL TO SAVE PROP. 13
Share Page
By Scott Kaufman, Legislative Director
This is the story of how the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association forced the Legislature into a near-unanimous vote to make it harder to raise taxes.
In the last weeks before the Legislature’s summer recess, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association was heavily pressured by special interest groups and elected officials, including the governor’s office, to pull the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 from the November ballot.
Many of our supporters in the business community received even more intense pressure, with demands that they stop helping HJTA’s campaign to pass the initiative. That led to the people concerned about transfer taxes cutting a separate deal for a transfer tax cap, introduced as Assembly Bill 736.
AB 736 was a terrible deal for taxpayers. It was not a constitutional amendment, so its caps on transfer taxes could be overridden with special legislation all the time, like the sales tax cap. And it did nothing at all about closing the “Upland” loophole, ambiguous language in the California Supreme Court’s 2017 California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland decision, which lower courts interpreted to allow special-interest-sponsored “citizens’ initiative tax increases” to evade the two-thirds vote requirement in Proposition 13.
HJTA was pressured to withdraw its initiative for AB 736 alone. But the problem with “Upland” taxes has been getting worse with every election, as more and more interest groups write their own tax increases, direct all the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then enjoy a much lower vote threshold to pass them than the identical measure would require if placed on the ballot by a government body: 50%-plus-1 instead of 66.67%.
Closing the “Upland” loophole has been a top priority for HJTA for almost 10 years. We cannot save Prop. 13 without closing the “Upland” loophole. We can’t fix transfer taxes without closing the “Upland” loophole. So, despite the pressure to withdraw the initiative in exchange for a transfer tax cap, and threats to spend upwards of $10 million against us if we didn’t, HJTA said no deal.
Then, with just hours to go before the deadline to finalize the ballot, we won a tremendous victory for taxpayers. The governor’s office and the Legislature reversed their previous stance and offered their full support for the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. They offered to pass a legislative constitutional amendment, Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, that would close the “Upland” loophole once and for all.
But that wasn’t enough. We also insisted that the Legislature reverse its vote from 2023 that put a “poison pill” constitutional amendment, Assembly Constitutional Amendment 13, on the November ballot. ACA 13 would have required the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 to meet an unusually high vote threshold to pass, potentially making it far more difficult to enact taxpayer protections through the initiative process, permanently.
The governor’s office and the Legislature agreed to our terms. Assembly Constitutional Amendment 21 was passed to remove the poison pill ACA 13 from the November ballot and clear the way for the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 to be approved by a simple majority of voters instead of a more challenging vote threshold. The new measure is exclusively focused on restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes in Proposition 13, after courts have eroded its protections.
That’s the deal to which HJTA agreed as a condition of withdrawing its original initiative.
In exchange, we deferred the fight over transfer taxes to another day, and we gave up the provision in the initiative that would have repealed, in two years, some existing transfer taxes and parcel taxes that court-created loopholes had already allowed.
On June 25, as the clock ticked down to the 5:00 p.m. deadline, the Assembly and the Senate voted almost unanimously to pass two Assembly Constitutional Amendments, ACA 21 and ACA 22, to put the revised Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 on the November ballot and take the poison pill ACA 13 off. HJTA was at the Secretary of State’s office to personally witness the measures being formally enrolled. When they could no longer be revoked, HJTA withdrew the original initiative.
As the legendary comedian W.C. Fields said, “Trust everybody, but cut the cards.”
After the 5:00 p.m. deadline, the Secretary of State officially certified all the November ballot measures. The Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 is now Proposition 43.
When voters approve it, all new local special taxes, those that earmark the revenue for specific purposes, will require a two-thirds vote of the people. This includes transfer taxes, sales taxes, business taxes and parcel taxes. There will no longer be an exception from the two-thirds vote requirement for any “citizens’ initiative tax increases” that were placed on the ballot by special interest groups collecting signatures.
The “Upland” loophole will finally be closed.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party

SUBJECT: Update on Ballot Initiative 25-0006A1: Limits Ability of Voters to Raise

The purpose of this memorandum is to provide an update on the statewide ballot
measure known as Initiative 25-0006A1: Limits Ability of Voters to Raise Revenues for
Local Government Services - Initiative Constitutional Amendment, and to summarize
the implications for the City of San José.
BACKGROUND
On June 16, 2026, the City Council adopted a resolution declaring the City’s opposition
to Initiative 25-0006A1, which was a proposed ballot measure to limit the ability of
voters to raise revenues for local government services.1 As described in the
Supplemental Memorandum to City Council on June 12, 2026, Initiative 25-0006A1
would decrease or eliminate real property transfer and conveyance taxes.2 The
Legislature and the Governor’s Office subsequently engaged in negotiations with the
ballot measure proponents to remove Initiative 25-0006A1 from the November 3, 2026
statewide general election by passing the legislation described below.
1 https://sanjose.legistar.com/View.ashx?M=F&ID=15582074&GUID=71E5A640-E2C2-462C-A2DD-
E1E4D5827DEB
2 https://sanjose.legistar.com/View.ashx?M=F&ID=15584662&GUID=FBD87519-0BA2-43DF-8F50-
AB2274742200
HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
June 30, 2026
Subject: Update on Ballot Initiative 25-0006A1: Limits Ability of Voters to Raise Revenues for Local
Government Services - Initiative Constitutional Amendment
Page 2
ANALYSIS
On June 25, 2026, the Legislature passed Assembly Constitutional Amendment (ACA)
22, which would require two-thirds of voters to approve a new or modified local special
tax, whether a citizen or an elected body initiated it, effective January 1, 2027.3 This
means no change to the existing two-thirds voter threshold for City Council-initiated
special taxes. However, citizen-initiated local ballot measures for special taxes, such as
the recent Santa Clara Valley Open Space Authority Measure D, would require a two-
thirds voter threshold.4
Additionally, ACA 22 would prohibit a local government, including the electorate of a
local government exercising the initiative power, from imposing ad valorem taxes on
real property, except as provided pursuant to Article XIII and Article XIIIA of the
California Constitution, with the same effective date. This change would not impact the
current two-thirds super majority voter approval requirement in the California
Constitution on local governments to increase ad valorem property tax for issuance of
general obligation bonds. Practically, this means that citizens cannot use a ballot
initiative to establish a new property tax based on the value of real property.
ACA 22 responds to the first condition from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association in
exchange for agreeing to remove Initiative 25-0006A1, and effectively nullifies the
California Supreme Court decision in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland
(2017). As a constitutional amendment, ACA 22 will appear on the November 3, 2026
ballot for voter approval, and requires a simple majority to pass. ACA 22 will not affect
other ballot measures already qualified for the November 3, 2026 ballot, including the
Connect Bay Area regional transit measure and the statewide Veterans and Affordable
Housing Bond.
The Legislature also passed ACA 21 on June 25, 2026, to fulfill a second condition from
the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to remove ACA 13 from the November 3,
2026 statewide general election.5 ACA 13 would have required an initiative
constitutional amendment that creates a supermajority voting requirement to win
approval by that same supermajority or not pass.
While ACA 22 fulfilled the two-third voter threshold envisioned in Initiative 25-0006A1, it
did not cap transfer taxes sought by the other two ballot measure proponents, the
California Business Roundtable and California Business Properties Association. These
entities, along with some pro-housing stakeholders, are exploring a legislative vehicle to
limit real property transfer taxes, such as Assembly Bill 736 (González). Assembly Bill
736 represented an initial compromise in exchange for removing Initiative 25-0006A1

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? ## Should local tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signature face a higher threshold if the tax will be used for a specific purpose?
Proposition 43 would make it harder to pass new local tax measures  by requiring a two-thirds vote to approve measures that earmark funds for a specific purpose, known as special taxes.
Currently, special taxes proposed by cities, counties or special districts need that supermajority approval, but as a result of a 2017 California Supreme Court ruling, special taxes proposed by voters require only a majority vote.
## Yes Argument
If a campaign wants to raise taxes for a specific purpose, it should have to win broad voter support.
Allowing a lower threshold for tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signatures is a loophole that has added to the tax burden facing Californians.

## No Argument
Local tax policy should not be governed by minority rule.
One-third of voters should not be able to overrule the majority who are willing to raise taxes for important local services.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

ESPAÑOL – MEDIDAS LOCALES: https://indivisibleventura.org/medidas-locales/ (https://indivisibleventura.org/medidas-locales/)
Protect your vote and majority rule!
What’s the Background? California’s Constitution lets local governments raise taxes only with local voter approval. A local tax dedicated to a specific purpose – a special tax – normally needs a two-thirds vote. But in its 2017 ruling in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland, the California Supreme Court held that the two-thirds rule DOES NOT apply when voters themselves put a special tax on the ballot by gathering signatures Those citizen-proposed measures pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would erase that distinction
How did this get on the ballot? Not by citizen signatures. Proposition 43 is Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, which the Legislature placed on the ballot in June 2026 as an eleventh-hour deal with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association – Jarvis agreed to pull an even more damaging initiative in exchange. Even its own author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) opposes it, and says she wrote it only to get the more dangerous measure off the ballot in time. No one is arguing that Proposition 43 is good policy. Special Interests want to control how and when we spend our money. They are not interested in improving the quality of life in our communities. They ARE interested in keeping money in their own pockets.
What would Proposition 43 do?
Raise the bar on citizen-proposed local special taxes from a simple majority (over 50%) to a two-thirds vote, beginning January 1, 2027.
Put the losing side in charge: a measure backed by 66% of voters – nearly two out of three – would be defeated by the 34% who voted no.
Make big money far more powerful: opponents would no longer need a majority, only one-third of the vote plus one – a much cheaper target to buy.
Make it harder to fund police and fire protection, road repairs, school staffing, and local hospitals and clinics – just as federal cuts to health care and other essential funding squeeze California hardest.
Bar local governments – and voters using the initiative – from imposing any new tax based on the assessed value of real property, apart from those the Constitution already allows.
Myths Facts
Proposition 43 restores protections originally approved under Proposition 13. This is a scare tactic meant to make voters think Proposition 43 protects their property taxes. It does not – taxes on the value of real property are a separate category from special taxes. Prop 43 does not change Prop 13 or your current property tax bill. It raises the approval threshold for certain local taxes and applies only to future measures. What it does do is take away your right to settle these questions by majority vote.
Proposition 43 lowers taxes and affirms your right to vote on local taxes. Proposition 43 DOES NOT cut taxes. It DOES limit the power of your vote. You already have the right to vote on every new or higher local tax. Proposition 43 simply raises the bar – letting 34% of voters veto what 66% of their neighbors want.
Proposition 43 is a new requirement for governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved. This is NOT a new requirement – it already existed. Special taxes are already legally restricted to the purpose voters approved – that is what makes them “special” taxes. Prop 43 adds no new spending safeguard at all. The only thing it changes is how many votes it takes to approve one.

Re: “Proposition 43 restores voters’ intent on taxes” (Page A6, Oct. 20).
In America, each person has one vote, and every vote counts equally.
Let’s protect majority rule by voting no on Proposition 43.
A yes vote would require a supermajority (2/3) for all taxes.
Special taxes, those intended for a specific purpose, require a simple majority.
Californians use special taxes to support public services like better police and fire protection, roads, libraries, parks, etc.
A two-thirds vote requirement undermines our democracy.
It means a third of voters can veto what taxes can be levied.
Is it fair to let a small minority determine election outcomes?
Should a minority of voters have more power than a majority vote?
That’s not democratic.
Reject Proposition 43.
I believe that a simple majority should be able to decide when to tax themselves for an important public service.
Let’s protect our democratic principles by preserving a simple majority vote when deciding important community issues.

Prop
43
CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.
Vote NO

by Max Dubler
Introduction
It should not take a supermajority of voters to raise revenues for local schools, infrastructure, and public safety.
Analysis
Background
Proposition 13, passed by voters in 1978, amended the state constitution to cap property tax rates at 1% of a property’s assessed value; limit annual increases in assessed value; require a ⅔ supermajority vote in the legislature to raise state taxes; and require a ⅔ voter approval for local “special taxes” earmarked for a specific purpose.
In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional supermajority requirements were written to constrain governments , not the people’s initiative power, and that “special” taxes that have been proposed via citizen initiatives can pass with a standard 50%+1 majority.
In 2022, Los Angeles voters passed Measure ULA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_ULA), which dramatically raised the transfer tax (https://finance.lacity.gov/faq/measure-ula) on real estate transactions over $5 million to up to 5.5%. Advertised to voters as a “mansion tax,” it has mostly affected the sales of apartment buildings and other commercial properties, leading to a very significant slowdown (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/the-unintended-consequences-of-measure-ula/) in large commercial property transactions and new housing construction (https://lewis.ucla.edu/research/taxing-tomorrow-measure-ulas-impact-on-multifamily-housing-production-and-potential-reforms/). San Francisco (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2020-11/sf-prop-i-transfer-tax-increase) and Santa Monica (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publication/230301-7087-santa-monica-measure-gs) have also passed significant transfer tax increases, with similar negative effects for housing.
Earlier this year, The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers’ Association (HJTA), which sponsored Prop 13 back in 1978, collected signatures for a ballot measure (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) that would do two things: restore the 66% supermajority requirement for special taxes and limit local transfer taxes to 0.055%. In June, the state legislature attempted to make a deal with the HJTA to keep this measure off the ballot by reforming transfer taxes, a laudable goal that we supported (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/06/mansion-tax-ballot-measure-deal/). That effort was not successful: negotiations broke down at the 11th hour (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/). When the dust settled, a deal was struck to have the legislature put the voter threshold piece on the ballot by itself without the transfer tax reforms. That is Prop 43.
What does this do?
Raises the threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing voter-approved special taxes from 50%+1 to 66% and prohibits local governments from taxing real estate according to its value, except under narrow circumstances.
How will this affect housing?
Prop 43 will impact housing production by making it harder for local governments to raise revenue for housing-related purposes like infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation.
Passing Prop 43 would also give local governments an even stronger incentive to charge very high impact fees for new housing (https://cayimby.org/reports/the-impact-of-fees/), which will increase the price of new homes and exacerbate the housing shortage.
Recommendation: No.
Kneecapping local governments’ ability to raise revenue is bad news for housing and infrastructure. Further, the HJTA should not be rewarded for using housing affordability as a Trojan horse to put unrelated tax cuts on the ballot.
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), initiative text (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22), “no” endorsement from transit advocacy group Seamless Bay Area (https://www.seamlessbayarea.org/blog/2026/7/10/prop-43-the-anti-tax-ballot-measure-and-transit-funding).

Endorsement: Back Prop. 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions on local taxes
Californians have already approved these limits twice, only to have courts erode the will of the electorate

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.
Related Articles
Endorsement: Break the 49ers’ grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose’s best choices (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.
